title: Incident Cadence Architects: Field Guide to On-call Rhythm, Drills, and Customer Notices
author: Maya Chen
content:
Title: Incident Cadence Architects: Field Guide to On-call Rhythm, Drills, and Customer Notices

Introduction
This guide describes the intended operational rhythm for on-call teams at Redwood Inference, and provides repeatable artifacts for designing incident cycles, game-day drills, customer status updates, and post-incident synthesis. It is intended for SREs, service owners, and engineering leads responsible for reliability and customer communication.

Purpose and scope
- Purpose: Define a repeatable cadence (detection -> stabilization -> restore -> learn) and provide concrete templates and metrics so teams can safely run experiments, measure improvement, and maintain customer trust.
- Scope: Applies to all Redwood customer-facing inference services (hosted API, Dedicated routing, Private control plane). Internal developer tools (CI runners, build cluster) should align but may have separate SLAs.

Table of contents
1) Principles
2) Roles and responsibilities
3) Incident cadence (detailed lifecycle)
4) Standard runbook template
5) On-call rotation patterns and handoff rules
6) Game-day and SLO-drill design
7) Customer status page and comms templates
8) Postmortem rubric and evidence checklist
9) Runbook maintenance and measurement
10) Appendices: CLI snippets and example escalation policy

1) Principles
- Prioritize user impact over internal alerts: categorize signals by customer-visible symptom first (API errors, latency increase, embedding quality regression).
- Keep the bridge lean: limit participants to necessary roles early; scale as severity requires.
- Safe experimentation: game days should be scripted with rollback plans and a pre-approved quiet window.
- Measure outcomes not effort: drills and postmortems should link to objective changes (SLOs, MTTR, automation coverage).

2) Roles and responsibilities
- Incident Commander (IC): owns decisions until handoff. Responsibilities: triage priority, approve temporary mitigations, coordinate external comms. Typical owner: senior SRE on rotation.
- Primary responder (Primary): first on-call engineer handling triage and initial mitigation.
- Secondary/Backup: supports primary, takes over for escalations and extended incidents.
- Service Owner / Product Liaison: provides feature/context and customer impact guidance.
- Communications Lead (Comms): crafts status page and external messages; often a member of CS or a designated SRE.
- Evidence Collector: records timestamps, commands run, metrics dashboards, and links to traces for later postmortem.

3) Incident cadence (detection -> closure)
1. Detection & Initial validation (0-5 minutes):
   - Alert fires (source: Prometheus, tracer-based SLI, customer report).
   - Primary acknowledges within 5 minutes. If no ack, PagerDuty escalates to Secondary.
   - Quick verification: run defined smoke-check commands (see Appendix A).
2. Triage & impact assessment (5-20 minutes):
   - IC identifies customer-visible symptoms, affected regions/tenants, estimated blast radius.
   - Categorize severity: Sev1 (customer-facing outage), Sev2 (degradation affecting >5% customers or p95 latency regression > 5x), Sev3 (minor or internal).
   - Record start time and notify stakeholders per escalation matrix.
3. Containment & mitigation (20-60 minutes):
   - Apply safe mitigations: routing fallbacks, capacity scaling, circuit breakers, or temporary feature disablement.
   - If mitigation requires cross-team action (DB, infra, routing), spin up bridge and assign owners.
4. Restore & verification (60-240 minutes):
   - Gradual roll-forward fixes with canary traffic where possible.
   - Monitor SLIs closely; when service meets recovery criteria (see SLI thresholds below), begin stakeholder notification of recovery.
5. Recovery & post-incident transition (240+ minutes):
   - Prepare a 1–2 paragraph incident summary for the status page.
   - Assign a postmortem owner within 48 hours.
6. Postmortem & follow-up (1–14 days):
   - Conduct blameless postmortem using the rubric below.
   - Publish action items and assign owners with due dates; tie to backlog and track until resolved.

Minimum SLIs and thresholds (example)
- Availability SLO (hosted API): 99.9% monthly availability. Error budget: 0.1% of requests per calendar month.
- Latency SLO: p95 generation latency < 200ms for short prompt workloads (<= 128 tokens); p99 < 700ms.
- Embedding throughput SLO: 99% requests complete within 800ms.
- Alert thresholds (examples): p95 latency increase > 2x baseline for 3m -> Severity 2 alert; error rate > 0.5% for 5m -> Severity 1 if customer impact confirmed.

4) Standard runbook template (use for service-level incidents)
- Title: short descriptive name (e.g., "api-inference-error-5xxs").
- Purpose: one sentence describing symptom being remedied.
- Owner: primary oncall and service team.
- Detection checks: list of dashboards/queries to run. Example: `curl -sS https://api.redwood.ai/health | jq .status` and `promql: sum(rate(http_request_errors[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests[5m]))`
- Quick mitigation steps (ordered):
  1. Identify if the problem is regional or global via region filtering.
  2. If caused by recent deploy, roll back the deploy (documented rollback command).
  3. If caused by capacity, scale Dedicated pool by +20% in the autoscale UI or use cli: `redwood scale --pool inference --delta 0.2` (example).
  4. If caused by model OOMs, switch traffic to quantized variant or compatible fallback model.
- Verification: list of metrics and thresholds to watch post-mitigation.
- Post-incident tasks: add test cases, update alert thresholds, create runbook improvements.

5) On-call rotation patterns and handoff rules
- Pattern A (default): 1-week primary shifts, weekday coverage 9am-6pm local, nights and weekends on-call with 24/7 rotation.
- Pattern B (high-intensity services): 2-week primary shifts with 24/7 on-call and a secondary for the first week of handover.
- Handoff checklist (must be completed for every shift change):
  1. Confirm completed incidents and outstanding action items.
  2. Review active alerts and silenced notifications.
  3. Share any planned maintenance or expected traffic spikes.
  4. Confirm escalation contact list and bridge URLs.
- Warm handoff protocol for long incidents: the outgoing primary briefs incoming primary in a 10-minute synchronous call and stays in observer role for first 30 minutes.

6) Game-day and SLO-drill design
- Objective: exercise the detection and mitigation workflow and measure time-to-first-action, MTTR, and false-positive tolerance.
- Planning steps:
  1. Define a scope and blast radius safe for production or use a staging mirror.
  2. Create a script with a clear failure injection and a documented rollback.
  3. Identify stakeholders and a Comms lead; schedule a quiet window where customer-impacting drills are allowed.
- Example drill: KV cache eviction and traffic spike
  - Expected learning: verify KV-cache warming strategy, observe autoscaler behavior, and validate alert thresholds for p95 latency.
  - Measured metrics: time to detect, time to mitigation, time to restore, number of manual steps.
- Post-drill: publish a short after-action report with measurable improvements and update runbooks.

7) Customer status page and comms templates
- Status page principle: fast, factual, and respectful. Use the template below and avoid speculative technical details.
- Message states (short forms used on status.redwood.ai):
  1. Investigating: We are aware of reports of [symptom]. Our team is investigating. (Examples: "Investigating: Increased API errors for text generation in us-west-2")
  2. Identified: We have identified a root cause and are implementing mitigation. (E.g., "Identified: Infrastructure routing misconfiguration affecting inference traffic")
  3. Mitigating: We are actively applying mitigations; service may be partially available.
  4. Restored: Service availability is restored; we are monitoring for stability.
  5. Postmortem published: A postmortem with findings and actions is available at [link].
- Status message template (short public update)
  - Title: Investigating: [short symptom]
  - Body: We are investigating reports of [symptom]. Affected customers may experience [impact]. We will provide an update within [timeframe].
- Escalated customer notice (to CS/enterprise)
  - Subject: Incident update – [service] – [time range]
  - Body: Hello (Customer Name),
    We are investigating an issue affecting [service]. Impact: [concrete symptom]. Mitigation in progress: [high-level steps]. We will share a timeline for resolution within [x] minutes and will follow up with a summary and corrective actions.

8) Postmortem rubric and evidence checklist
- Postmortem timeline: draft published within 72 hours.
- Required sections:
  1. Summary (1–2 paragraphs)
  2. Impact (customers, regions, tenant count)
  3. Root cause analysis (what happened and why)
  4. Timeline of actions (timestamps and actors)
  5. Mitigations and rollbacks applied
  6. Action items (owner, priority, due date)
  7. Lessons learned and preventive measures
- Evidence checklist (must be attached or linked):
  - Alert payloads and Prometheus query results.
  - Relevant logs and sampling of trace IDs.
  - Deployment diffs (commit IDs) if deploy-related.
  - PagerDuty timeline and acknowledgement logs.
  - Customer support tickets and status page history.

9) Runbook maintenance and measurement
- Runbook ownership: every runbook has an owner and an annual review date. Owners will tag runbooks with `last-tested` after any game day or real incident.
- Key metrics to track annually per service:
  - Mean time to acknowledge (MTTA) target: < 5 minutes.
  - Mean time to mitigate (first effective mitigation): < 30 minutes for Sev1s.
  - Mean time to restore (MTTR): < 120 minutes for Sev1s.
  - Automation coverage: % of mitigation steps executable via documented CLI or playbook target > 70%.
- Quarterly cadence: each service must run at least one SLO-drill or game day per quarter. Results are summarized during the reliability review.

10) Appendices
A) Quick validation commands (examples)
- Health check: `curl -sS https://api.redwood.ai/health | jq .status`
- Error rate (Prometheus): `sum(rate(http_request_errors[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests[5m]))`
- Check model serving pool occupancy: `redwood-admin pool list --service inference`

B) Example Slack public-facing status snippet (30 minute update)
- `@channel: INVESTIGATING: We are aware of increased 5xx errors for inference in us-west-2. Engineers are investigating. We will update in 30 minutes. Link: <status.redwood.ai/incident/xxxx>`

C) Example escalation policy (pseudo-YAML)
- `escalation_policy:`
  - `- after: 5m -> notify: secondary`
  - `- after: 15m -> notify: oncall-lead and IC`
  - `- after: 60m -> page: director-oncall`

D) Measuring improvement: example post-drill KPIs
- Reduction in manual steps required in runbook (baseline vs post-action).
- Decrease in MTTR across three subsequent incidents.
- Increase in automation coverage (playbooked steps).

Owner and next steps
- Document owner: Maya Chen (SRE).
- Next review scheduled: 2024-05-01.
- Action: Teams should use this guide to plan their next quarterly SLO-drill and tag runbooks with `last-tested` when complete.

Feedback
Please add suggestions directly to the page comments or file a PR against the runbook template in the operations docs repo.
